summary: A glossary of policy-related terms with abbreviations, explanations, and recommendations, intended to improve consistency in writing about network policy.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines terms used in network policy documents. It gives writers and readers a shared vocabulary for concepts such as policy rules, decision points and enforcement points.

questions: what is a policy decision point
what is the difference between pdp and pep
what is a policy rule in networking
subtitle: Definitions and usage guidance for common terms in network policy documents.

tldr.problem: Network policy documents may use the same words in different ways, making them harder to understand and compare.
tldr.mechanism: The memo provides an alphabetical glossary with definitions, abbreviations, source references and recommendations for using policy terminology.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3198 is an Informational glossary intended to improve consistency in Internet Standards documents. It does not define a protocol.

today: RFC 3198 is an Informational glossary. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Policy Glossary
sections.content:
RFC 3198 is a glossary of policy-related abbreviations, definitions and explanations. Its goal is to make Internet Standards documents, including RFCs and Internet-Drafts, easier to understand and more consistent.

Where possible, the glossary takes definitions from existing documents and identifies their sources. When more than one definition exists, it lists each one with its source. Expired Internet-Drafts are not used as sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary helps technical documents use policy terms consistently. It usually points to existing definitions rather than creating new ones.

sections.title: Entry Labels and Cross-References
sections.content:
Entries are listed alphabetically, and only proper nouns are capitalized. Each definition paragraph has a label: P marks basic policy terms, T marks techniques for creating or conveying policy information, and A marks work groups or general areas where policy is used.

Some entries point to technology-specific terms without defining them. Readers are directed to the cited document for those details.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels tell readers what kind of entry they are reading: a policy idea, a technique or an area of use. Cross-references direct readers to other definitions.

sections.title: Policies, Rules and Errors
sections.content:
The glossary defines a policy rule as a set of conditions bound to a set of actions. If its conditions are met, the actions are performed. A policy condition states whether actions should run; a policy action states what should be done.

A policy conflict occurs when two satisfied rules require contradictory actions. A policy error occurs when an action cannot be enforced, for example because of temporary state or a mismatch with a device's capabilities. The glossary also describes policy goals, levels of abstraction and translation between policy representations.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy rule says what conditions trigger an action. A conflict means two rules disagree; an error means the selected action cannot be carried out.

sections.title: Decision and Enforcement Roles
sections.content:
A Policy Decision Point (PDP) makes policy decisions for itself or for network elements that ask for them. A Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces those decisions. A message from a PEP to a PDP is more precisely called a policy decision request.

The glossary distinguishes outsourced policy, where a device asks an external component for a decision when an event occurs, from provisioned policy, where a device receives configuration in advance. These execution models are not mutually exclusive. The entry calls “policy server” an imprecise term.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDP decides what a policy requires, and a PEP carries out the decision. A device may ask for a decision when needed or receive policy settings in advance.

sections.title: Information and Data Models
sections.content:
An information model describes entities, their properties and their relationships without depending on a particular repository, protocol or platform. A data model maps that information into a form for a particular type of data store.

The glossary also defines management and provisioning terms, including MIB, Policy Information Base (PIB), Provisioning Class (PRC) and Structure of Policy Provisioning Information (SPPI). It notes that PRC means Provisioning Class because these objects describe configuration data, not if/then rules.
sections.plainLanguage: An information model describes what things exist and how they relate. A data model specifies how to represent that information in a particular kind of store.
